evidence.title: Neuro-Symbolic Verification of LLM Outputs for Data-Sensitive Domains (extended preprint)

evidence.quote: In contrast, the verifier agent restores 100% accuracy by blocking adversarial consensus.

evidence.title: ETHOS: Towards a Modular Ethics Framework for Clinical Multi-Agent Systems

evidence.title: Large language models approach clinician performance in ESC cardiovascular risk stratification: a vignette-based benchmark study

evidence.effect: Deterministic κw 0.85-0.90 versus original 0.15-0.61 in eligible vignettes; all eleven models improved, Δκw +0.29 to +0.72.

evidence.title: Standard guardrails impose a safety-critical omission tax on clinical large language models that a downstream verification layer reverses: a retrospective multi-cohort evaluation

evidence.quote: A downstream verification layer that modified the response before it was returned lowered omission to the bare-model level (paired reduction 16.46 percentage points; Newcombe 95% confidence interval 10.93 to 21.86; McNemar exact P = 1.32 × 10⁻²³), detected 49.0% of the omissions the guardrails missed, and missed none that the guardrails caught (per-model 39.8% to 73.3%; P < 10⁻⁴).

evidence.title: Prompt-Induced Output Variability and Structured-Output Integrity in Local Open Large Language Models: A Multi-model In Silico Benchmark Using Synthetic Acute-Care Scenarios
evidence.outcome: cross-field structured-output inconsistency
evidence.effect: Gemma had 0 invalid outputs, but T3 top-action argmax agreement fell to 0.389-0.397.

evidence.sample_unit: synthetic acute-care cases (3 timepoints, 21 prompt variants, 3 runs, 3 models)

commentary.bottom_line: Most tests of automated output checks ran offline or in simulation, where the checks caught fabricated entities and implausible values at reported detection rates between 72% and 100%. Two small real-deployment reports and one mixed result on harmful errors suggest the checks reduce errors but do not remove them when no human reviews the output.

perspectives.view: In a 25-case ablation, 166 deterministic rules eliminated all 6 fabrication failures, and red-flag routing cut vignette safety violations from 8/56 to 0/56. An LLM-judge filter left harmful errors nearly unchanged for o3 (4.3% to 3.9%). A drug-name dictionary check missed some drug error categories because of dictionary limits and misspellings.

Performance varied by output type. Deterministic SCORE2 recalculation raised agreement from κw 0.15-0.61 to 0.85-0.90, and rule-based verification raised accuracy from 64.9% to 74.8%. An image screener flagged synthetic CT hallucinations at specificity 0.78 to 0.98 depending on a distance parameter, which suggests thresholds may need local tuning before use.

Portuguese vignettes and Korean clinical records showed gains in agreement and accuracy after checks, and emergency vignettes from Japan showed fewer safety violations. A fourth study used Japanese safety reports translated to English. None enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, low-literacy, or US limited English proficiency patients, so performance for those groups is unknown.

CHAI states that teams should add a human to the workflow or else implement additional quality control processes. FUTURE-AI recommends mechanisms to detect implausible outputs without tying this to the absence of human review. Neither source sets performance thresholds, and no supplied study evaluates checks against a regulatory standard.

One deployment report described a 30% reduction in report creation time with automated verification. A postprocessing filter cut order set suggestions by 29% while keeping 92% of useful ones, and an offline regeneration step reduced signal loss from 15.55% to 8.48% without extra LLM calls. Staffing and rule-maintenance costs were not reported.

The LLM-judge filter replaced flagged answers with a deferral to a provider, which gives patients a route to a human. Harmful errors still appeared in 3.9% to 7.6% of simulated responses after filtering, so patients may need to be told that automated checks lower risk but do not remove it.

commentary.research_gap: No randomized or controlled prospective study compares deployed AI with and without automated checks on patient outcomes. Future work should measure errors that reach patients, false alarm burden on staff, and rule maintenance costs in live deployments, including settings that serve Medicaid and limited English proficiency patients.
commentary.underserved_note: Two tests used Portuguese vignettes or Korean clinical records, one used emergency vignettes from Japan, and one used Japanese safety reports translated to English, which offers limited evidence that checks work outside US English-language data. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, low-literacy, or US limited English proficiency patient populations, so health systems serving those groups cannot assume the reported detection rates will hold and may need to validate checks locally.
